title: Three Against Three
teaser: Only one on-site review slot remained for Friday, yet both Hongchuan and Qisheng had file bags marked “three.” If bad news were counted one item at a time, the two companies were tied. What changed the visiting order was what happened after the information entered one index under common definitions.
paragraphs: On Wednesday afternoon, the field team told Lin Lan that only one on-site review slot remained that week, on Friday morning. Hongchuan and Qisheng were both still under normal credit status; neither had already defaulted, and whichever firm was not visited that week would remain in the ordinary monitoring queue. Lin Lan’s task was not to stop anyone’s lending. With limited review capacity, she only had to decide which company should be checked first. She placed two transparent file bags side by side on her desk: Hongchuan on the left, Qisheng on the right.

She began with the fastest manual method and pulled three conspicuous pieces of bad news from each set of statements. Hongchuan showed high leverage, weak working capital, and a loss for the year. Qisheng had current liabilities above current assets, losses in two consecutive years, and profit that had deteriorated further from the previous year. She stuck a yellow label on the mouth of each bag and wrote the same thing on both: “three.” Hongchuan’s leverage looked harsher; Qisheng’s losses had lasted longer. By eye alone, it was difficult to say which group of three weighed more. Lin Lan left the Friday visit sheet between the two bags and did not let any single item decide.

She then recalculated the inputs according to the bank’s model card. Total liabilities had to be scaled by total assets, and working capital had to follow the prescribed definition. Net income, funds from operations, current liabilities and current assets, whether equity was negative, consecutive losses, and changes in profit were all checked back against the original statements. Firm size was entered exactly as the model defined it, rather than being interpreted separately as “large means safe” or “small means risky.” The yellow labels stayed in place because “three” recorded only the number of items a person had selected; it was not the weight assigned to the model inputs.

Before sending the data into the system, Lin Lan checked the population and prediction horizon one more time. This version had already been revalidated on a group of similar firms within the bank, and both companies fell within its intended use. The system did not add up another score for the “three” items. Instead, different variables entered the same linear index with estimated coefficients, and the index was then converted into a probability between zero and one. When the results appeared, Hongchuan showed 6% and Qisheng 24%. On the desk, it was still three against three. On the screen, the risks were no longer tied.

Lin Lan did not respond by opening any option to stop lending, reduce the facility, or begin a disposal process. Twenty-four percent was not a verdict on Qisheng’s fate, and six percent did not remove Hongchuan from monitoring. She only slipped the single Friday visit sheet into Qisheng’s bag. On the checklist she added recent orders, collections, short-term repayment arrangements, and sources of cash. Hongchuan stayed in the normal queue for the next review opportunity. The model changed the order in which scarce investigative resources were used, not the current credit status.

On Thursday evening, the field supervisor came to collect the materials. Lin Lan placed Qisheng’s transparent bag into the briefcase while Hongchuan’s remained on the desk. Just before the lid closed, one corner of the old yellow label was still visible, still reading “three.” Right beside it, in the upper-right corner of the on-site visit sheet, was printed “24%.”
concept: The Ohlson financial-distress probability model combines size, leverage, liquidity, profitability, cash flow, and several status indicators into a linear index using coefficients estimated from a sample, then maps that index to a probability between zero and one through a logit transformation. Because the variables differ in definition, direction, and weight, the model cannot be replaced by simply counting how many red flags appear.
explanation: Three pieces of bad news can be selected manually for both Hongchuan and Qisheng, but “three” shows only that the counts are equal; it does not mean that the information has the same definition, severity, or combined effect. Once the inputs are put on a common basis, the variables jointly form an index using estimated coefficients, producing the difference between 6% and 24%.
mapping: Both file bags are labelled “three” → the same number of red flags does not imply the same statistically estimated distress risk.
Size, leverage, liquidity, profitability, cash flow, and other inputs are recalculated according to the model card → one model must use consistent variable definitions.
Different variables enter the linear index and then pass through a logit transformation → 6% and 24% arise from the combination and weights, not from simple counting.

The 24% company receives the first on-site review while its credit status remains unchanged → probability can help prioritise investigation, but it is not an individual destiny or an automatic action.
boundary: The original Ohlson study was developed for a particular sample and prediction horizon. In practice, users must check whether the population, time frame, variable definitions, and coefficients match the case at hand, and the model will usually require revalidation or recalibration. Its probability represents statistical risk, not the certainty that a particular firm will enter distress; review priority may also depend on exposure, collateral, and other management considerations.
reflection: If both bags contain only “three” pieces of bad news, why can the model still assign Friday’s single on-site review slot to one company rather than the other?

calculation.note: Illustrates only the logit transformation mechanism; it does not represent the actual regression inputs of the companies in the story
